topics.name: Lee Harvey Oswald
topics.kicker: Accused assassin of John F. Kennedy · Shot by Jack Ruby two days later
topics.briefing: On November 22, 1963, Lee Harvey Oswald, a former Marine who had once moved to the Soviet Union, was arrested in a Dallas movie theater and charged with assassinating President John F. Kennedy and killing police officer J. D. Tippit. Two days later, nightclub owner Jack Ruby shot Oswald on live television before he could stand trial. In 1964, the Warren Commission concluded that Oswald had acted alone.
topics.answerHtml: Lee Harvey Oswald (do not accept “Jack Ruby” or “John F. Kennedy”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After serving as a radar operator in the U.S. Marines, this man moved to the Soviet Union in 1959 and worked at a radio factory in Minsk. There he married Marina Prusakova, and in 1962 he brought her back to Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who, the Warren Commission concluded, assassinated President John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: In August 1963, this man was arrested in New Orleans after a street scuffle while he was handing out leaflets for the pro-Castro Fair Play for Cuba Committee. Weeks later, he traveled to Mexico City and visited the Cuban consulate and the Soviet embassy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former Marine who was arrested in a Dallas movie theater on November 22, 1963.

tossups.p: The Warren Commission concluded that this man had tried to shoot the retired general Edwin Walker at Walker’s Dallas home in April 1963. That fall, this man took a job at a warehouse that stored schoolbooks, overlooking Dealey Plaza.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man accused of assassinating President John F. Kennedy from that building, the Texas School Book Depository.

tossups.p: A shoe store manager named Johnny Brewer saw this man step into his store’s entrance as police cars went by, then slip into the nearby Texas Theatre without buying a ticket. Police arrested this man inside, not long after Dallas officer J. D. Tippit had been shot and killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who was charged with assassinating John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: On November 24, 1963, this man was being moved through the basement of Dallas police headquarters on his way to the county jail when he was shot. He died at Parkland Hospital, the same hospital where the president had died two days earlier.
tossups.r: His killer, nightclub owner Jack Ruby, shot him on live television. For 10 points, name this man accused of assassinating John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: Chief Justice Earl Warren led a commission that concluded in 1964 that this man had acted alone, and that this man’s own killer had also acted alone. Future president Gerald Ford served on that commission.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who, the commission found, assassinated President Kennedy from a window of the Texas School Book Depository.

tossups.p: This man carried a fake identity card in the name “Alek James Hidell,” and he rented a room in Dallas under the name “O. H. Lee.” In October 1963, Ruth Paine, a friend of his wife’s, helped him get a job at a schoolbook warehouse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who, the Warren Commission found, assassinated John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: Don DeLillo [“duh-LIL-oh”] imagined the life of this man, who was born in New Orleans in 1939, in the novel _Libra_. In Stephen King’s novel _11/22/63_, a high school teacher travels back in time hoping to stop this man.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man whom the Warren Commission named as the assassin of John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: The Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza occupies the floor of a Dallas warehouse where this man worked. The Warren Commission found that he fired at the president’s motorcade from a corner window on that floor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former Marine accused of assassinating John F. Kennedy in 1963.

tossups.p: Soon after arriving in Moscow in 1959, this former Marine went to the American embassy and announced that he wanted to give up his U.S. citizenship. He returned to the United States in 1962 with his Russian wife and their baby daughter, June.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who was arrested the next year for the assassination of John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: About 45 minutes after shots were fired in Dealey Plaza, Dallas police officer J. D. Tippit stopped this man on a street in the Oak Cliff neighborhood and was shot and killed. The Warren Commission concluded that this man killed Tippit.
tossups.r: Earlier that day, President John F. Kennedy had been assassinated. For 10 points, name the man charged with both crimes.

tossups.p: Former CIA director Allen Dulles and Georgia senator Richard Russell served on a commission that Lyndon Johnson created in November 1963 to investigate a crime this man was accused of. That commission concluded in 1964 that this man had acted alone.
tossups.r: It was led by Chief Justice Earl Warren. For 10 points, name this man accused of assassinating John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: This man’s killer was born Jacob Rubenstein in Chicago and ran a Dallas nightclub. District Attorney Henry Wade’s office won a murder conviction against that killer in 1964, but the killer died in 1967 while awaiting a new trial.
tossups.r: That killer was Jack Ruby. For 10 points, name this man whom Ruby shot, the accused assassin of John F. Kennedy.

tossups.p: This man joined the U.S. Marines in 1956, just after turning 17, and served at an air base in Japan. He taught himself Russian while still in the Marines, and after leaving the service in 1959 he headed for the Soviet Union.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who, the Warren Commission concluded, shot President Kennedy from the Texas School Book Depository.

tossups.p: Texas governor John Connally was wounded in the 1963 attack that this man was accused of carrying out, while riding in the same open car as the president through Dealey Plaza. Moments earlier, Connally’s wife, Nellie, had said, “Mr. President, you can’t say Dallas doesn’t love you.”
tossups.r: Two days later, this man was shot by Jack Ruby. For 10 points, name this man charged with assassinating John F. Kennedy.

clues.t: Accused of assassinating President John F. Kennedy in Dallas on November 22, 1963
Shot two days later by nightclub owner Jack Ruby, before he could stand trial
Worked at the Texas School Book Depository, which overlooks Dealey Plaza
The Warren Commission (1964) concluded that he acted alone
A former U.S. Marine who moved to the Soviet Union (1959–1962)
Married Marina Prusakova in Minsk and brought her back to Texas in 1962
Arrested in the Texas Theatre, a Dallas movie theater
Also charged with killing Dallas police officer J. D. Tippit, who was shot that same afternoon
The commission found the shots came from a sixth-floor window of the depository, where the Sixth Floor Museum is
Chief Justice Earl Warren led the commission, which Lyndon Johnson created; future president Gerald Ford was a member
Ruby shot him in the Dallas police basement on live television (November 24, 1963)
Handed out leaflets for the pro-Castro Fair Play for Cuba Committee in New Orleans (1963)
Visited the Cuban consulate and the Soviet embassy in Mexico City (fall 1963)
The commission found he had tried to shoot retired general Edwin Walker in April 1963
Used the false names “Alek James Hidell” (on a fake ID card) and “O. H. Lee”
Got the depository job in October 1963 through Ruth Paine, a friend of his wife’s
Born in New Orleans (1939); joined the Marines at 17 and served at an air base in Japan
Told the U.S. embassy in Moscow he wanted to give up his citizenship (1959); worked at a radio factory in Minsk
Shoe store manager Johnny Brewer saw him slip into the theater without buying a ticket
Jack Ruby, born Jacob Rubenstein, was convicted in 1964 (prosecuted by Henry Wade’s office) and died in 1967 awaiting a new trial
Died at Parkland Hospital, where Kennedy had died two days earlier
Officer Tippit was killed in Dallas’s Oak Cliff neighborhood about 45 minutes after the shots in Dealey Plaza
Commission members also included former CIA director Allen Dulles and Senator Richard Russell
Don DeLillo’s novel _Libra_ imagines his life; in Stephen King’s _11/22/63_, a time traveler tries to stop him
Texas governor John Connally was wounded riding in the same car as Kennedy

trap.title: Assassin, Killer, or Event?
trap.body: The same clues, like Dealey Plaza, the Texas School Book Depository, and the Warren Commission, show up in three answer lines: Lee Harvey Oswald (the accused assassin), Jack Ruby (the nightclub owner who shot Oswald), and the assassination of John F. Kennedy (the event). Answering “Kennedy” to a question about the gunman is wrong, and so is answering “Ruby” to a question about the man Ruby shot.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man” or “this former Marine,” with clues about the Soviet Union, Minsk, or the Texas Theatre, wants Oswald; “this nightclub owner,” or a man born Jacob Rubenstein, wants Jack Ruby; “this event” wants the assassination of John F. Kennedy. Don’t mix him up with John Wilkes Booth, who shot Abraham Lincoln in 1865.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lee Harvey Oswald (do not accept “Jack Ruby” or “John F. Kennedy”)

topics.name: Manifest Destiny
topics.kicker: Belief that the U.S. was meant to span the continent · Named in 1845
topics.briefing: In 1845, the editor John L. O’Sullivan wrote that it was America’s “manifest destiny” to spread across the whole continent. In the same decade, the United States annexed Texas, split the Oregon Country with Britain, and took California and the Southwest after the Mexican-American War. That growth came at a heavy cost to Native American nations and to Mexico, and it sharpened the fight over slavery.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: An 1845 magazine essay supporting the annexation of Texas spoke of America’s mission “to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions.” That essay appeared in the _Democratic Review_, edited by John L. O’Sullivan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phrase for the belief that the United States should expand from coast to coast.

tossups.p: In an 1872 painting by John Gast, a giant floating woman named Columbia carries a schoolbook and strings telegraph wire as she leads settlers west, while Native Americans and buffalo flee ahead of her. That painting, _American Progress_, is often used to illustrate this idea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that Americans were meant to spread across North America.

tossups.p: Expansionists demanded all of the Oregon Country, up to latitude 54 degrees 40 minutes north, with the cry “Fifty-four forty or fight!,” but the 1846 Oregon Treaty divided the region with Britain along the 49th parallel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, championed by President James K. Polk, that the United States should stretch from coast to coast.

tossups.p: James Gadsden negotiated an 1853 deal that paid Mexico 10 million dollars for land in present-day southern Arizona and New Mexico, which was wanted for a railroad route. That purchase was the last big piece of land added to the lower 48 states in the era of this idea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, popularized by John L. O’Sullivan in 1845, that the United States should spread across North America.

tossups.p: During the Civil War, Emanuel Leutze [“LOYT-suh”], better known for painting Washington crossing the Delaware, completed a U.S. Capitol mural celebrating this idea, titled _Westward the Course of Empire Takes Its Way_, in which pioneers cross the Rocky Mountains toward the Pacific.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, named in 1845, that the United States should expand to the Pacific Ocean.

tossups.p: The adventurer William Walker carried this idea south when he made himself president of Nicaragua in 1856. Private soldiers like Walker, who tried to seize land in Latin America without government approval, were called filibusters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this idea, made famous by John L. O’Sullivan in 1845, that the United States was meant to expand.

tossups.p: During the Mexican-American War, some believers in this idea backed an “All Mexico” movement to annex the entire defeated country. Instead, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo gave the United States California and most of the Southwest.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, championed by President James K. Polk, that the U.S. should span North America.

tossups.p: In the last days of his presidency, John Tyler signed a joint resolution of Congress to annex Texas, a move cheered by expansionists who held this belief. Months later, the phrase naming this idea appeared in an essay about Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1840s belief that the United States had a mission to expand to the Pacific.

tossups.p: A president who embraced this idea set four goals for his single term, including settling the Oregon question and acquiring California, and he achieved all of them. That president had won the 1844 election over the Whig Henry Clay.
tossups.r: That president was James K. Polk. For 10 points, name this belief that Americans had a God-given mission to spread across North America.

tossups.p: Many supporters of this idea claimed that American settlers would make better use of Western land than the Native American nations and Mexican citizens who already lived there. Westward expansion pushed many Native nations off their homelands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, pictured in John Gast’s _American Progress_, that the U.S. should stretch from coast to coast.

tossups.p: After the 1890 census reported that the frontier line had disappeared, some Americans revived this idea to argue for expansion overseas. In 1898, the United States annexed Hawaii and gained the Philippines from Spain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, first named in 1845, that the United States was meant to expand.

tossups.p: Whigs such as Henry Clay distrusted this idea, partly because they feared that new territory in the Southwest would spread slavery. The fight over the Wilmot Proviso, which tried to ban slavery in land won from Mexico, split Congress along sectional lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, championed by Democrats like James K. Polk, that the United States should expand to the Pacific.

tossups.p: Thousands of families caught “Oregon fever” in the 1840s and set out from Independence, Missouri, on a trail of about 2,000 miles to the Pacific Northwest, a migration encouraged by this idea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief, named in 1845, that Americans were meant to settle the continent from coast to coast.

tossups.p: In a December 1845 newspaper article about the Oregon dispute with Britain, an editor claimed the right “to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent which Providence has given us.” That editor, John L. O’Sullivan, ran the _New York Morning News_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phrase he used for the belief that the United States should stretch from sea to sea.

tossups.p: In 1846, American settlers in Sonoma raised a flag showing a grizzly bear and declared California independent from Mexico, and the explorer John C. Frémont [“FREE-mont”] soon took charge of their revolt. Believers in this idea hoped to add California to the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this belief that the United States should expand all the way to the Pacific Ocean.

clues.t: The 1840s belief that the United States was meant to expand across North America, from the Atlantic to the Pacific
A phrase made famous by the editor John L. O’Sullivan in 1845
President James K. Polk (1845–1849) was its great champion
Used to justify the Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
John Gast’s painting _American Progress_ (1872): Columbia floats west, stringing telegraph wire
“Fifty-four forty or fight!”: expansionists demanded all of the Oregon Country, up to latitude 54°40′ north
Oregon Treaty (1846): split the Oregon Country with Britain at the 49th parallel
The annexation of Texas (1845)
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848): the Mexican Cession added California and most of the Southwest
Gadsden Purchase (1853): $10 million for southern Arizona and New Mexico, for a railroad route
Westward expansion pushed many Native American nations off their homelands
“Oregon fever”: families took the Oregon Trail west from Independence, Missouri
The 1845 essay spoke of a mission “to overspread the continent allotted by Providence”; it ran in the _Democratic Review_
O’Sullivan’s December 1845 _New York Morning News_ article used the phrase in the Oregon dispute
Polk’s four goals: lower tariffs, an independent treasury, Oregon, and California; he met them all in one term
John Tyler signed the joint resolution to annex Texas just before leaving office (March 1845)
The “All Mexico” movement wanted to annex the whole country after the war
Emanuel Leutze’s Capitol mural _Westward the Course of Empire Takes Its Way_, painted during the Civil War
In Gast’s painting, Columbia carries a schoolbook while Native Americans and buffalo flee ahead of her
The filibuster William Walker made himself president of Nicaragua (1856)
Bear Flag Revolt (1846): American settlers in Sonoma declared California independent; John C. Frémont took charge
Whigs such as Henry Clay distrusted it, fearing war and the spread of slavery; the Wilmot Proviso fight followed
Supporters claimed American settlers would make better use of the land than the Native nations and Mexicans living there
After the 1890 census said the frontier line was gone, the idea was revived for overseas expansion, such as annexing Hawaii (1898)

trap.title: Destiny or Doctrine?
trap.body: Manifest Destiny and the Monroe Doctrine both describe American power in the Western Hemisphere, so players swap them. The Monroe Doctrine (1823) was President James Monroe’s warning that Europe should not set up new colonies in the Americas; Manifest Destiny (1845) was the belief that the United States itself should spread across North America. Frederick Jackson Turner’s 1893 “Frontier Thesis” is a third, later idea about what the frontier meant for American democracy.
trap.fix: Dates and names sort them out: 1823, Monroe, John Quincy Adams, and keeping Europe out mean the Monroe Doctrine; 1845, O’Sullivan, Polk, Texas, Oregon, and coast-to-coast expansion mean Manifest Destiny; 1893, Turner, and the closing of the frontier mean the Frontier Thesis.
trap.line: Real answer line: Manifest Destiny (do not accept “Monroe Doctrine”)

topics.name: Plymouth Colony
topics.kicker: Founded by the Mayflower Pilgrims in 1620 · Site of the 1621 harvest feast
topics.briefing: In December 1620, about 100 passengers from the _Mayflower_ began building a settlement on the coast of present-day Massachusetts. About half of them died that first winter, but with help from Squanto and a peace treaty with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, Plymouth Colony survived and held a famous harvest feast in 1621. Governed for decades by William Bradford, it became part of Massachusetts in 1691.
topics.answerHtml: Plymouth Colony (or Plimoth or New Plymouth; prompt on Pilgrims; do not accept “Massachusetts Bay Colony,” “Jamestown,” “Mayflower,” or “Plymouth Rock”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In March 1621, an Abenaki [“AB-uh-NAH-kee”] man named Samoset walked into this settlement and greeted its colonists in English. He soon returned with Squanto, who taught the settlers to plant corn using fish as fertilizer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded in 1620 by Pilgrims who had sailed on the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: Many founders of this colony had moved to the Dutch city of Leiden [“LYE-den”] in 1609 so they could worship freely as Separatists. When they sailed for America, their other ship, the _Speedwell_, leaked so badly that they left it behind.
tossups.r: They crossed the Atlantic on the _Mayflower_ instead. For 10 points, name this colony founded in 1620 in present-day Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Peregrine White, born aboard ship in Cape Cod Harbor in November 1620, is remembered as the first English child born in New England, weeks before his family helped found this colony. Another passenger, Oceanus Hopkins, had been born at sea during the same voyage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded by Pilgrims who had sailed from England on the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: In 1621, the Wampanoag [“wahm-puh-NOH-ag”] leader Massasoit agreed to a treaty of peace and mutual defense with this colony, and the alliance lasted for more than fifty years. Squanto served as an interpreter during the talks.
tossups.r: That fall, Massasoit and about 90 of his men joined the colonists for a three-day harvest feast. For 10 points, name this colony remembered for that “first Thanksgiving.”

tossups.p: Edward Winslow described a three-day gathering at this colony in a 1621 letter printed in _Mourt’s Relation_, writing that the Wampanoag guests went out and killed five deer for the colony’s governor.
tossups.r: That gathering was a harvest feast often called the first Thanksgiving. For 10 points, name this colony, founded by the Pilgrims.

tossups.p: This colony never received a royal charter of its own, and in 1691 a new charter from King William III and Queen Mary II made it part of the Province of Massachusetts Bay. Before that, Edmund Andros had ruled it as part of the Dominion of New England.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony founded in 1620 by Pilgrims who sailed on the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: In 1628, Myles Standish arrested Thomas Morton, whose nearby trading post at Merrymount angered this colony’s leaders with a maypole celebration and with trading guns to Native Americans, and Morton was shipped back to England.
tossups.r: Standish was the military leader of this colony. For 10 points, name this colony governed for many years by William Bradford.

tossups.p: After two hungry years of farming in common, Governor William Bradford gave each family in this colony its own plot of land in 1623, and harvests improved. Bradford later wrote a history of this colony in which he called its founders “pilgrims.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony settled in 1620 by passengers of the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: The handwritten history of this colony by its longtime governor disappeared from Boston during the American Revolution. Decades later it turned up in a library in London, and it was returned to Massachusetts in 1897.
tossups.r: That governor, William Bradford, led this colony for about thirty years. For 10 points, name this colony founded by the Pilgrims.

tossups.p: One Native helper of this colony had been kidnapped by an English captain in 1614 and taken to Spain to be sold into slavery, but he made his way to England and back home, only to find that disease had wiped out his Patuxet [“puh-TUX-et”] village. This colony was built on that village’s site.
tossups.r: That helper was Squanto. For 10 points, name this colony founded in 1620 by Pilgrims from the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: John Carver was chosen as this colony’s first governor right after he and 40 other men signed an agreement to make “just and equal laws.” Carver died the next spring and was replaced by William Bradford.
tossups.r: That agreement was the Mayflower Compact. For 10 points, name this colony founded by the Pilgrims.

tossups.p: In a Henry Wadsworth Longfellow poem, a soldier of this colony sends his friend John Alden to propose to Priscilla Mullins for him, and she replies, “Why don’t you speak for yourself, John?”
tossups.r: That soldier, Myles Standish, led this colony’s militia. For 10 points, name this colony founded by Pilgrims who sailed on the _Mayflower_.

tossups.p: Captain Christopher Jones’s ship first anchored off the tip of Cape Cod, near present-day Provincetown, in November 1620, but its passengers soon moved across the bay to found this colony. About half of those settlers died during the first winter.
tossups.r: That ship was the _Mayflower_. For 10 points, name this colony founded by the Pilgrims.

tossups.p: In 1741, a 94-year-old church elder named Thomas Faunce pointed out a granite boulder that he said marked the spot where this colony’s founders had first stepped ashore. That boulder was later broken in two while people tried to move it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony whose famous “Rock” is said to mark the Pilgrims’ landing place.

tossups.p: Massasoit’s son Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, went to war against the New England colonies in 1675, after this colony executed three Wampanoag men for the death of John Sassamon.
tossups.r: That war ended the alliance Massasoit had made with this colony in 1621. For 10 points, name this colony founded by the Pilgrims.

clues.t: Founded in 1620 by the Pilgrims, who sailed from England on the _Mayflower_
In present-day Massachusetts; it became part of the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691
Its 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is often called the first Thanksgiving
Squanto (Tisquantum) taught the colonists to plant corn, using fish as fertilizer
Mayflower Compact (1620): 41 men agreed to make “just and equal laws” before going ashore
William Bradford governed it for about thirty years and wrote its history
John Carver was its first governor; he died in the spring of 1621
Massasoit, a Wampanoag leader, made a 1621 peace treaty with the colony that lasted more than 50 years
Samoset walked into the settlement in March 1621 and greeted the colonists in English
Myles Standish, a soldier, led its militia
About half of the colonists died during the first winter
The Pilgrims were Separatists, who broke away from the Church of England
Many founders had lived in Leiden, in the Netherlands; their leaky ship _Speedwell_ was left behind
The _Mayflower_, captained by Christopher Jones, first anchored near present-day Provincetown on Cape Cod
Peregrine White, born aboard the _Mayflower_, was the first English child born in New England; Oceanus Hopkins was born at sea
Squanto had been kidnapped in 1614 and taken to Spain; disease wiped out his Patuxet village, where the colony was built
Edward Winslow’s 1621 letter in _Mourt’s Relation_: Massasoit and about 90 men feasted with the colonists for three days
In 1623, Bradford gave each family its own plot of land instead of farming in common
Bradford’s handwritten history vanished during the Revolution and was returned from London in 1897
It never had a royal charter of its own; Edmund Andros ruled it in the Dominion of New England (1686–1689)
Standish arrested Thomas Morton of Merrymount (1628), known for his maypole
Longfellow’s poem about Standish: John Alden and Priscilla Mullins (“Why don’t you speak for yourself, John?”)
In 1741, elder Thomas Faunce pointed out the granite boulder said to mark the landing place
King Philip’s War (1675–1676), led by Massasoit’s son Metacom, began after the colony executed three Wampanoag men
Roger Williams lived in the colony for about two years before he founded Providence

trap.title: Colony, Ship, or Rock?
trap.body: Plymouth Colony shares clues with several other answer lines. The _Mayflower_ was the ship, and the Mayflower Compact was the agreement signed aboard it; Massachusetts Bay Colony was a separate, larger Puritan colony founded around Boston in 1630 that absorbed Plymouth in 1691; and Jamestown (1607, Virginia) was England’s first permanent colony in North America. Saying “Plymouth Rock” when the question wants the colony is wrong too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This colony” with the Pilgrims, Bradford, Squanto, Massasoit, or the 1621 harvest feast means Plymouth; “this ship” means the _Mayflower_; “this document” means the Mayflower Compact; John Winthrop, Boston, and the “city upon a hill” mean Massachusetts Bay. John Smith, Pocahontas, and tobacco mean Jamestown.
trap.line: Real answer line: Plymouth Colony (or Plimoth; prompt on Pilgrims; do not accept “Massachusetts Bay Colony” or “Plymouth Rock”)

topics.name: Pullman Strike
topics.kicker: 1894 railroad strike led by Eugene V. Debs · Ended by federal troops
topics.briefing: During an economic depression in 1893 and 1894, the Pullman Palace Car Company, which built fancy railroad sleeping cars, cut its workers’ wages but refused to lower the rents they paid to live in the company town it had built on Chicago’s South Side. When the workers walked out, Eugene V. Debs’s American Railway Union refused to handle trains carrying Pullman cars, and rail traffic stalled across much of the country. President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops, and the strike collapsed.
topics.answerHtml: Pullman Strike (or Pullman Boycott; prompt on railroad strike; do not accept “Haymarket Affair” or “Homestead Strike”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Jane Addams compared the businessman at the center of this event to Shakespeare’s King Lear in her essay “A Modern Lear.” She had tried to help settle this dispute, which began after that man’s company cut its workers’ wages without lowering their rents.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 railroad strike led by Eugene V. Debs and his American Railway Union.

tossups.p: In the 1895 case _In re Debs_, the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the use of a federal court order to end this strike. Clarence Darrow defended the union leader who was jailed for ignoring that order.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike against a company that built railroad sleeping cars.

tossups.p: Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld, who had pardoned three men convicted after the Haymarket affair, protested when the president sent federal troops to Chicago during this strike. The president said the troops were needed to keep the U.S. mail moving.
tossups.r: That president was Grover Cleveland. For 10 points, name this 1894 strike against a railroad car company.

tossups.p: Attorney General Richard Olney, a former railroad lawyer, won a court order against the leaders of this strike, arguing that they were blocking the mail and interstate commerce. That order relied partly on the Sherman Antitrust Act.
tossups.r: Federal troops arrived in Chicago soon after. For 10 points, name this 1894 railroad strike led by Eugene V. Debs.

tossups.p: The town at the center of this event had its own church, library, and a hotel named for the company founder’s daughter, Florence, but workers could only rent their homes from the company. When business slowed in 1893, the company cut wages but did not lower rents.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike that began among workers who built railroad sleeping cars.

tossups.p: Over the objections of its president, the union that led this strike voted in 1894 to keep Black workers out of its membership. Earlier that year, the same union had won a strike against James J. Hill’s Great Northern Railway.
tossups.r: That union was the American Railway Union. For 10 points, name this strike led by Eugene V. Debs.

tossups.p: While serving six months in a jail in Woodstock, Illinois, for his role in this strike, a union leader read socialist writings. He later ran for president five times as a socialist, once while he was in prison.
tossups.r: That leader was Eugene V. Debs. For 10 points, name this 1894 strike against a railroad car company.

tossups.p: A federal commission led by Carroll Wright investigated this strike and criticized the company at its center for refusing to settle the dispute through arbitration. That same year, Congress made Labor Day a national holiday.
tossups.r: President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago to end this strike. For 10 points, name this 1894 railroad strike.

tossups.p: During the hard times that followed the Panic of 1893, a company that built luxurious railroad sleeping cars cut its workers’ pay but kept charging the same rent for the company-owned houses they lived in.
tossups.r: Its workers walked out in May 1894. For 10 points, name this strike, which spread across the nation’s railroads when Eugene V. Debs’s union joined it.

tossups.p: During this strike, a group of railroad executives called the General Managers’ Association had mail cars attached to trains carrying sleeping cars, so that stopping those trains would interfere with the U.S. mail.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike that began among workers who built sleeping cars in Chicago.

tossups.p: Meeting in Chicago in July 1894, Samuel Gompers and other leaders of the American Federation of Labor refused to call a general strike in support of this strike, which collapsed after its leaders were arrested.
tossups.r: Its leader, Eugene V. Debs, headed the American Railway Union. For 10 points, name this 1894 strike against a maker of railroad sleeping cars.

tossups.p: In 1898, four years after this strike, the Illinois Supreme Court ruled that running a town was beyond the powers of the company at the strike’s center and ordered it to sell the homes it owned. That company’s founder had died the year before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike that Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to break.

tossups.p: In 2015, Barack Obama made part of the neighborhood where this strike began into a national monument. That neighborhood on Chicago’s South Side had been a company town, where workers had to rent their homes from their employer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike led by Eugene V. Debs’s American Railway Union.

tossups.p: The same spring that Jacob Coxey led a march of unemployed men to Washington, D.C., workers at a sleeping-car factory in Chicago began this strike. It spread nationwide that summer when their new union refused to handle the company’s cars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike led by Eugene V. Debs and broken by federal troops.

tossups.p: Starting on June 26, 1894, after the company refused to arbitrate, a union ordered its members not to handle any train that pulled the company’s sleeping cars, and the boycott soon stopped traffic on many rail lines west of Chicago.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1894 strike, which President Grover Cleveland ended by sending federal troops.

clues.t: Nationwide railroad strike and boycott of 1894
Led by Eugene V. Debs and his American Railway Union
President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago to end it
Began among workers who built railroad sleeping cars in a company town on Chicago’s South Side
Cause: in the hard times after the Panic of 1893, the company cut wages but did not lower rents
_In re Debs_ (1895): the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the court order used to end the strike
Debs went to jail for ignoring the court order (an injunction) and became a socialist
Cleveland said troops were needed to keep the U.S. mail and interstate commerce moving
That same year (1894), Congress made Labor Day a national holiday, and Cleveland signed the law
Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld protested the use of federal troops
Attorney General Richard Olney got the court order, partly under the Sherman Antitrust Act
The union refused to handle any train pulling the company’s cars, stopping traffic on many lines west of Chicago
Jane Addams compared the company’s founder to King Lear in her essay “A Modern Lear”
Clarence Darrow defended Debs
Debs read socialist writings during six months in jail in Woodstock, Illinois, and later ran for president five times
The American Railway Union had won a strike against James J. Hill’s Great Northern Railway earlier in 1894
The American Railway Union voted to keep out Black workers, over Debs’s objection
The railroads’ General Managers’ Association had mail cars attached to trains carrying sleeping cars
Samuel Gompers and the American Federation of Labor refused to call a general strike to support it
Altgeld had pardoned three men convicted after the Haymarket affair (1893)
A federal commission led by Carroll Wright investigated and criticized the company for refusing to arbitrate
In 1898, the Illinois Supreme Court ordered the company to sell the homes in its town; the founder had died in 1897
The company town had a hotel named for the founder’s daughter, Florence; part of it became a national monument in 2015
Coxey’s Army of unemployed men marched to Washington the same spring

trap.title: Pullman, Haymarket, or Homestead?
trap.body: Three famous labor clashes of the late 1800s get mixed up. The Haymarket affair (1886, Chicago) began when a bomb exploded at a labor rally; the Homestead Strike (1892, Pennsylvania) was a fight at one of Andrew Carnegie’s steel mills, where Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards; and the Pullman Strike (1894) was a nationwide railroad boycott. The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 was an earlier rail strike.
trap.fix: Listen for the year and the names: Debs, the American Railway Union, sleeping cars, Grover Cleveland’s troops, and _In re Debs_ mean Pullman; Haymarket Square and anarchists mean Haymarket; Carnegie, Frick, and the Pinkertons mean Homestead; Rutherford B. Hayes and 1877 mean the Great Railroad Strike.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pullman Strike (or Pullman Boycott; do not accept “Haymarket Affair” or “Homestead Strike”)
